question: Let $X$ be a finite set containing $n$ elements and let $f:X\to X$ be an onto function. Prove that $f$ must necessarily be one-one.
explanation:
Given condition
The set $X$ contains $n$ elements and $f:X\to X$ is onto. Therefore, every one of the $n$ elements of the co-domain $X$ must occur as the image of at least one element of the domain.

Contrary assumption
Suppose that $f$ is not one-one. Then there exist two distinct elements $x_1,x_2\in X$ such that $$x_1\neq x_2\quad\text{but}\quad f(x_1)=f(x_2)$$ Thus, two of the $n$ elements of the domain have the same image.

Effect on the range
The remaining $n-2$ elements of the domain can contribute at most $n-2$ further distinct images. Together with the common image of $x_1$ and $x_2$, the range can therefore contain at most $$1+(n-2)=n-1$$ distinct elements.

Contradiction with onto property
Since the co-domain $X$ contains $n$ elements, an onto function must have all $n$ elements in its range. But the assumption that $f$ is not one-one gives at most $n-1$ elements in the range. This contradicts the fact that $f$ is onto.

Final Result
Hence, the assumption that $f$ is not one-one is false. Therefore, every onto function $f:X\to X$ on a finite set $X$ is necessarily one-one.

options.A: An onto function $f:X\to X$ need not be one-one because two elements of the domain may have the same image while every co-domain element still has a pre-image.
options.B: The conclusion holds only when $n$ is even; for odd values of $n$, an onto function need not be one-one.
options.C: The function must be constant because the domain and co-domain are the same finite set.
options.D: The function must be one-one because if two distinct domain elements had the same image, the range would contain at most $n-1$ elements, contradicting the onto property.
